claims.claim: Compared with placebo, quinine reduces the number of cramps modestly: about 2 to 3 fewer cramps over two weeks from about 9 on placebo (about a quarter fewer), on low-quality evidence.
claims.supporting_passage: Cochrane 2015, Effects of interventions: "Quinine resulted in a significant decrease in cramp number (-2.45 cramps, 95% CI -3.54 to -1.36, random-effects), equivalent to a 28% (95% CI 15% to 40%) reduction over placebo (see Analysis 1.2, Figure 2). It is worth noting the persistent heterogeneity (I2 = 71%) associated with this result." Summary of findings table: "The mean number of cramps over 2 weeks in the control groups was 8.8 cramps"; "The mean number of cramps over 2 weeks in the intervention groups was 2.45 lower (1.36 to 3.54 lower)" [952 participants, 13 studies, GRADE low]. Cramp days: "The remaining seven trials (n = 842) showed that quinine significantly reduced cramp days compared to placebo (-1.15 days, 95% CI -1.93 to -0.38, random-effects) (see Analysis 1.6). This represents a 20% (95% CI 6% to 33%) reduction in cramp days". Abstract: "There is low quality evidence that quinine (200 mg to 500 mg daily) significantly reduces cramp number and cramp days and moderate quality evidence that quinine reduces cramp intensity." Man-Son-Hing 1998, Abstract: "When individual patient data from all crossover studies were pooled, persons had 3.60 (95% confidence interval [CI] 2.15, 5.05) fewer cramps in a 4-week period when taking quinine compared with placebo." Table 3: placebo "17.08 (15.40, 18.76)" cramps per 4-week period (n = 409).
claims.location: Cochrane: Results (Effects of interventions, quinine versus placebo), Summary of findings table 1, Abstract. Man-Son-Hing: Abstract, Results, Table 3.
claims.pico_timeframe: People with muscle cramps (mostly idiopathic night cramps; trial mean ages 44 to 76) / quinine 200 to 500 mg daily / placebo / number of cramps, cramp days, intensity / two-week treatment period (trials up to 60 days)
claims.safe_wording: In pooled trials, people on a dummy tablet had about 9 cramps in two weeks. People on quinine had about 2 to 3 fewer, so roughly 6 or 7 instead of 9. That is about a quarter fewer cramps, and the evidence is low quality. Cramps were only slightly less painful.
claims.qualifications: Give the absolute figures first; the 28% is relative. Say the evidence is low quality. Trials were short (up to 60 days) and included some middle-aged adults, not only older people. 'About 6 or 7' is derived by subtracting 2.45 from 8.8. The intensity effect was small (0.12 points on a 3-point scale, from 1.2).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: High heterogeneity (I2 71%). Man-Son-Hing 1998 showed that published trials overstated the benefit (8.83 fewer cramps per 4 weeks in published trials vs 3.60 when unpublished data were added). The Cochrane review states there is no evidence to judge the best dose or duration.

numbers.meaning: mean cramps over 2 weeks in placebo groups (Cochrane SoF; 13 trials, 952 participants)
absolute mean difference in cramps over 2 weeks, quinine vs placebo
relative reduction in cramp number vs placebo (2.45 of 8.8)
absolute and relative reduction in days with cramps over 2 weeks (7 trials, n = 842)
cramp intensity, quinine vs placebo (7 trials, n = 666)
Man-Son-Hing 1998: mean cramps per 4 weeks on placebo and absolute reduction on quinine, pooled crossover trials (n = 409)

claims.claim: In trials, minor side effects (mainly stomach upset) were slightly more common with quinine; the trials were too small and short to measure rare serious harms.
claims.supporting_passage: Abstract: "A significantly greater number of people suffered minor adverse events on quinine than placebo (risk difference (RD) 3%, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0% to 6%), mainly gastrointestinal symptoms. Overdoses of quinine have been reported elsewhere to cause potentially fatal adverse effects, but in the included trials there was no significant difference in major adverse events compared with placebo (RD 0%, 95% CI -1% to 2%). One participant suffered from thrombocytopenia (0.12% risk) on quinine." Authors' conclusions: "There is moderate quality evidence that with use up to 60 days, the incidence of serious adverse events is not significantly greater than for placebo in the identified trials, but because serious adverse events can be rarely fatal, in some countries prescription of quinine is severely restricted." ... "Because serious adverse events are not common, large population studies are required to more accurately inform incidence."
claims.pico_timeframe: Trial participants with cramps / quinine / placebo / minor and major adverse events / up to 60 days
claims.safe_wording: In the trials, about 3 more people in every 100 had minor side effects on quinine than on a dummy tablet, mostly stomach upset. The trials lasted up to about two months and were too small to measure rare serious harms.
claims.qualifications: The 3 in 100 is an absolute risk difference (95% CI 0 to 6). 'No significant difference in major adverse events' in short trials must not be read as 'safe'.

numbers.meaning: absolute risk difference for minor adverse events, quinine minus placebo
absolute risk difference for major adverse events in trials up to 60 days
thrombocytopenia on quinine across included trials

claims.claim: Quinine can rarely cause serious harm, including immune reactions that destroy platelets (thrombocytopenia), heart rhythm problems especially in overdose, and death in overdose; dose-related side effects are a particular concern in older people.
claims.supporting_passage: Cochrane 2015, Background: "Quinine may have potentially serious adverse effects including fatal hypersensitivity reactions, particularly quinine-induced thrombocytopenia (Barr 1990) which can occur idiosyncratically from the ingestion of even minimal amounts of quinine, such as are present in commercial tonic waters (Schneemann 2006). Other hypersensitivity reactions include angio-oedema, disseminated intravascular coagulation, pancytopenia (Maguire 1993) and haemolytic uraemic syndrome (McDonald 1997)." ... "Quinine can interfere with the conduction pathways in the heart giving rise to arrhythmias, especially in overdosage (White 2007). Acute intoxication (ingestion of 4 to 12 g quinine) can cause convulsions followed by coma; death from respiratory arrest often results with doses exceeding 8 g." Plain language summary: "Quinine can cause serious, even fatal adverse events, especially in overdosage." Discussion: "A case-control study in the USA estimated that quinine-induced thrombocytopenia occurs in 26 of every 1 million users (Kaufman 1993)." Rabbitt 2016, Abstract: "However, the degree of benefit from quinine is modest and the risks include rare but serious immune-mediated reactions and, especially in older people, dose-related side effects."
claims.location: Cochrane: Background (Description of the intervention), Plain language summary, Discussion (Adverse events due to quinine). Rabbitt: Abstract.
claims.pico_timeframe: Quinine users (therapeutic use and overdose) / serious adverse reactions / background and case-report literature summarised by the reviews
claims.safe_wording: Quinine can rarely cause serious reactions. These include a sudden fall in platelets, the blood cells that help clotting, and heart rhythm problems, especially after too many tablets. An overdose of quinine can kill. A review in Age and Ageing notes that older people are more prone to its dose-related side effects.
claims.qualifications: These harms come from case reports, regulatory data and a case-control study summarised in the Cochrane background and discussion, not from the review's own trial results. If the 26 per million figure is used, attribute it to a US case-control study (Kaufman 1993) cited by the Cochrane review, and do not present it as a Cochrane finding. Do not quote the MHRA's list of harms (not opened).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: True incidence of serious harm at usual doses is uncertain; the review calls for large population studies.

numbers.meaning: estimated incidence of quinine-induced thrombocytopenia from a US case-control study (Kaufman 1993) cited in the Cochrane discussion; background figure, not the review's finding

claims.claim: Guidance restricts quinine for cramps to severe symptoms, as a trial with regular review; UK advice reported in the Cochrane review allows up to 4 weeks to see an effect and a pause every 3 months to check benefit; the MHRA issued a quinine safety update in June 2010.
claims.supporting_passage: Rabbitt 2016, Abstract: "Quinine treatment should be restricted to those with severe symptoms, should be subject to regular review and requires discussion of the risks and benefits with patients." Cochrane 2015, Discussion: "The British National Formulary (BNF) advises that it may take up to four weeks for the effect on cramp to become apparent and that if there is improvement, then quinine should be taken continuously with close monitoring for adverse events (BNF 2010). The BNF also advises interruption of treatment every three months for review of benefit." Man-Son-Hing 1998, Discussion: "If this fails and the patient's quality of life is significantly affected, then a trial of quinine (of at least 4 weeks) may be warranted. As with all potentially hazardous medications, physicians prescribing quinine need to closely monitor the benefits and risks in individual patients." Acheampong 2013, Abstract: "To ascertain the effects of the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency's (MHRA) safety update in June 2010 on the volume of prescribing of quinine and on indices of quinine toxicity."
claims.location: Rabbitt: Abstract. Cochrane: Discussion (Other considerations). Man-Son-Hing: Discussion. Acheampong: Abstract (Aims).
claims.pico_timeframe: People with night cramps considered for quinine / prescribing guidance / review of benefit at about 4 weeks and every 3 months
claims.safe_wording: Specialists in older people's medicine advise keeping quinine for severe cramps, reviewing it regularly and talking through benefits and risks (Age and Ageing review, 2016). UK prescribing advice reported in the Cochrane review said the effect can take up to 4 weeks to show, and treatment should be paused every 3 months to check it is still helping. The UK medicines regulator issued safety advice on quinine for cramps in 2010.
claims.qualifications: The MHRA 2010 Drug Safety Update was not opened: do not quote its wording (for example 'not for routine use' or 'stop after 4 weeks if no benefit') as MHRA text. The BNF advice is the 2010 edition as reported by Cochrane; the current BNF was not opened, so say 'UK prescribing advice' rather than quoting the current BNF.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Cochrane: 'There is no evidence to judge optimal dosage or duration of quinine treatment.'

numbers.meaning: time for effect to become apparent (BNF 2010 as reported by Cochrane); trial of at least 4 weeks (Man-Son-Hing)
interruption of treatment to review benefit (BNF 2010 as reported by Cochrane)
date of MHRA quinine safety update

claims.claim: MHRA (June 2010): quinine not for routine use for nocturnal leg cramps; consider only when cramps severely disrupt sleep, are very painful or frequent, other causes are ruled out and non-drug measures have failed; review after 4 weeks.
claims.supporting_passage: Search-engine summary only (not an opened document): "The update stated that quinine should not be used routinely for nocturnal leg cramps." ... "treatment with quinine should only be considered when cramps cause severe disruption of sleep, and should only be used when cramps are very painful or frequent, other treatable causes of cramp are ruled out and symptoms are not alleviated by non-drug measures, such as passive stretching exercises." ... "Treatment should be reviewed after 4 weeks to see whether there is any benefit and monitor for toxicity."
claims.location: WebSearch result summary (GPonline, MIMS pages not opened)
claims.pico_timeframe: UK prescribing of quinine for nocturnal leg cramps / regulatory advice / 2010
claims.safe_wording: Do not attribute this wording to the MHRA in the post. Use the wording in C10-03-d instead.
claims.qualifications: search_extract only; not sufficient for an essential claim. Consistent with the opened sources (Rabbitt 2016, Cochrane 2015, Man-Son-Hing 1998).

numbers.meaning: review point reported for the MHRA advice (search extract only)

claims.claim: After the 2010 MHRA advice, quinine prescribing in England stopped growing but remained common; areas with comprehensive prescribing reviews saw much larger reductions.
claims.supporting_passage: "Total prescribing continued to increase, but annual growth in quinine prescribing in England declined from 6.0 to -0.6% following the MHRA update [difference -0.04 (95% confidence interval -0.07 to -0.01) quinine prescriptions per 100 patients per quarter, P = 0.0111]. Much larger reductions were observed in Primary Care Trusts that introduced comprehensive prescribing reviews." ... "The MHRA advice was followed by limited reductions in the growth in quinine prescribing and in indicators of quinine overdose and toxicity. Quinine prescribing, however, remains common, and further efforts are needed to reduce availability and use."
claims.pico_timeframe: Primary care prescribing in England / before vs after MHRA June 2010 update / quinine prescribing volume and poisons enquiries / 2007/8 to 2011/12
claims.safe_wording: After the 2010 UK safety advice, quinine prescribing in England stopped rising but stayed common, at least to 2012. Areas that ran thorough prescribing reviews saw much larger falls.
claims.qualifications: Data end in 2012; current prescribing levels were not checked. Ecological before-and-after data: the review programmes are linked with larger falls, not proven to cause them. This contradicts the draft opening line that quinine 'is no longer a routine prescription in the UK'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No more recent UK prescribing data were opened.

numbers.meaning: annual growth in quinine prescribing in England before vs after the June 2010 MHRA update

claims.claim: In a UK primary care trial, advising people on long-term quinine to try stopping it led more of them to stop, without a clear difference in cramps at 12 weeks.
claims.supporting_passage: "One hundred and ninety-one patients prescribed quinine for night cramps were randomised to one of four groups defined by two 'advice' factors: undertake exercises and stop quinine." ... "At 12 weeks there was no significant difference in number of cramps in the previous 4 weeks (exercise = 1.95, 95% confidence interval [CI] = -3.01 to 6.90; quinine cessation = 3.45, 95% CI = -1.52 to 8.41) nor symptom burden or severity of cramps. However, after 12 weeks 26.5% (95% CI = 13.3% to 39.7%) more patients who had been advised to stop quinine treatment reported taking no quinine tablets in the previous week (odds ratio [OR] = 3.32, 95% CI = 1.37 to 8.06)" ... "Advising those on long-term repeat prescriptions to try stopping quinine temporarily will result in no major problems for patients, and allow a significant number to stop medication."
claims.pico_timeframe: 191 people on repeat quinine for night cramps, 28 English general practices / advice to stop quinine / no such advice / quinine use and cramp frequency / 12 weeks
claims.safe_wording: In a trial in 28 English general practices, people on long-term quinine were randomly given advice to try stopping it, or not. At 12 weeks, about 1 in 4 more of those advised to stop were taking none, and the trial did not show a clear difference in how many cramps people had.
claims.qualifications: The cramp comparison had wide confidence intervals and cannot rule out some rise in cramps for some people. Say 'did not show a clear difference', not 'no effect'. 26.5% is a difference in percentage points. Do not use the 3.45 figure (direction of the difference is not clear from the abstract).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Small trial from 2005; outcome relied on recalled cramp counts.

numbers.meaning: patients randomised
more people taking no quinine in the previous week at 12 weeks, advised to stop vs not

claims.claim: Stretching before bed is a low-risk option, but evidence that it reduces night cramps is limited and mixed.
claims.supporting_passage: Hawke 2021, Abstract: "A combination of daily calf and hamstring stretching for six weeks may reduce the severity of night-time lower limb muscle cramps (measured on a 10 cm visual analogue scale (VAS) where 0 = no pain and 10 cm = worst pain imaginable) in people aged 55 years and older, compared to no intervention (mean difference (MD) -1.30, 95% confidence interval (CI) -1.74 to -0.86; 1 RCT, 80 participants; low-certainty evidence). The certainty of evidence was very low for cramp frequency" ... "Calf stretching alone for 12 weeks may make little to no difference to the frequency of night-time lower limb muscle cramps in people aged 60 years and older" ... "No participant in these three studies reported adverse events. The evidence for adverse events was of moderate certainty as the studies were too small to detect uncommon events." Coppin 2005, Conclusions: "Calf-stretching exercises are not effective in reducing the frequency or severity of night cramps." Rabbitt 2016, Abstract: "There is conflicting evidence regarding the efficacy of prophylactic stretching exercises in preventing cramps."
claims.location: Hawke: Abstract (Main results, Authors' conclusions). Coppin: Abstract (Conclusions). Rabbitt: Abstract.
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults aged 50 and over with night cramps / calf or calf plus hamstring stretching / no intervention or sham stretching / cramp frequency and severity / 6 to 12 weeks
claims.safe_wording: Evidence on stretching is limited and mixed. In one small trial in people aged 55 and over, calf and hamstring stretches before bed for six weeks may have made cramps less painful; whether they came less often is very uncertain. In another, calf stretches alone made little or no difference. No one in these trials reported harm, so stretching is reasonable to try, but it is not a proven treatment.
claims.qualifications: The candidate's claim that stretching 'reduced the frequency and severity' (Hallegraeff 2012 alone) overstates the evidence; present stretching as low-risk to try. Do not use the Hallegraeff '1.2 cramps per night' figure (very low certainty).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Hallegraeff 2012 (positive, 80 people not on quinine) vs Coppin 2005 (negative, people on quinine); Cochrane grades certainty very low to low.

numbers.value: 1.3 cm lower on a 10 cm pain scale (95% CI 0.86 to 1.74)
numbers.meaning: cramp severity, calf plus hamstring stretching vs nothing, 6 weeks, 1 trial of 80 people aged over 55 (low certainty)

claims.claim: Some medicines are linked with night cramps, particularly thiazide-type and potassium-sparing diuretics and long-acting beta-agonist inhalers.
claims.supporting_passage: Garrison 2012, Abstract: "Adjusted sequence ratios (95% CIs) for the 3 drug classes were 1.47 (1.33-1.63 [P < .001]) for diuretics, 1.16 (1.04-1.29 [P = .004]) for statins, and 2.42 (2.02-2.89 [P < .001]) for LABAs. For diuretic subclasses, adjusted sequence ratios (95% CIs) were 2.12 (1.61-2.78 [P < .001]) for potassium sparing, 1.48 (1.29-1.68 [P < .001]) for thiazidelike, and 1.20 (1.00-1.44 [P = .07]) for loop." ... "Cramp treatment was substantially more likely in the year following introduction of LABAs, potassium-sparing diuretics, or thiazidelike diuretics, and 60.3% of quinine users (individuals experiencing cramp) received at least 1 of these medications during a 13-year period. In contrast, statin and loop diuretic associations were small." Rabbitt 2016, Abstract: "Recent evidence suggests that diuretic and long-acting beta-agonist therapy predispose to leg cramps."
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults aged 50 and over, British Columbia / starting diuretics, statins or LABAs / quinine starts in year before vs year after / 2000 to 2008
claims.safe_wording: Some medicines are linked with night cramps. In a large Canadian study of adults aged 50 and over, new treatment for cramps was more common in the year after starting some water tablets (thiazide-type and potassium-sparing diuretics) or long-acting inhalers for the lungs. The link with statins and loop diuretics was small. This kind of study shows a link, not proof that the medicine caused the cramps.
claims.qualifications: Observational; quinine starts are a proxy for cramps. Do not convert sequence ratios into 'X times more likely'. Never suggest stopping a diuretic or inhaler without advice; the action is to ask a doctor or pharmacist.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Canadian prescribing 2000 to 2008; UK practice may differ.

numbers.meaning: adjusted sequence ratios for LABAs, potassium-sparing and thiazide-like diuretics (ratio of quinine starts in year after vs year before starting the drug)
adjusted sequence ratios for statins and loop diuretics (small associations)
quinine users who received at least one of LABA, potassium-sparing or thiazide-like diuretic over 13 years

claims.claim: Co-codamol (codeine with paracetamol) and co-dydramol (dihydrocodeine with paracetamol) contain paracetamol; co-codamol 8/500 is sold in UK pharmacies without prescription.
claims.supporting_passage: Methods, Definitions: "compound overdose described overdose of compound tablets which included paracetamol such as co-proxamol or co-dydramol." Results: "Of the 48 subjects who had consumed an overdose of compound analgesics, the majority (21/48, 43.8%) had used codeine phosphate/paracetamol compounds (co-codamol), an analgesic available over the counter (OTC) in pharmacies in the UK at a dose of 8/500 mg, and only by prescription at higher doses. A total of 14 subjects had overdosed on prescribed compound analgesics, namely dextropropoxyphene/paracetamol (co-proxamol, n = 7) and dihydrocodeine tartrate/paracetamol (co-dydramol, n = 7)."
claims.location: Methods (Definitions); Results (Repeated supratherapeutic overdoses and pain)
claims.pico_timeframe: Definition of product composition (UK, as described in 2012)
claims.safe_wording: Co-codamol is codeine plus paracetamol. Co-dydramol is dihydrocodeine plus paracetamol. The lowest-strength co-codamol can be bought in UK pharmacies without a prescription.
claims.qualifications: OTC status is as described in 2012; not rechecked against current UK rules. Do not name brands.

numbers.meaning: co-codamol strength (8 mg codeine, 500 mg paracetamol) available over the counter in UK pharmacies, per Craig 2012

claims.claim: Some cold and flu remedies also contain paracetamol.
claims.supporting_passage: Chidiac 2024, Table 1 (Paracetamol involved): "Cold and flu preparations: Entire cohort: 1726 (12.0%)"; Results 3.1: "This was closely followed by combinations with opioids (primarily consisting of paracetamol and codeine with just 0.7% paracetamol and tramadol) and cold and flu preparations (which often include other ingredients including decongestants and sedating antihistamines)." Wolf 2012, Table 3 secondary products shown in the double-dipping scenarios include "Brand Name Combination Cold & Cough (650 mg/dose)" [acetaminophen dose].
claims.location: Chidiac: Table 1 and Results 3.1. Wolf: Methods and Table 3.
claims.pico_timeframe: Paracetamol-containing products involved in dosing errors (Australia 2017 to 2023) and in a US simulated dosing study
claims.safe_wording: Some cold and flu remedies also contain paracetamol, so check the ingredients list on anything you buy for a cold.
claims.qualifications: Sources describe Australian and US products; UK packs were not examined. Say 'some', not 'most' or 'many'.

numbers.meaning: share of Australian paracetamol dosing-error calls that involved cold and flu preparations, 2017 to 2023

claims.claim: The usual maximum daily dose of paracetamol for adults is 4 g in 24 hours.
claims.supporting_passage: Reid 2022, Introduction: "Although paracetamol-induced hepatotoxicity at standard therapeutic doses (up to 4 g/d) is rare, cases have been reported." Craig 2012, Methods (Definitions): "a staggered overdose described ingestion of two or more supratherapeutic paracetamol doses over a time interval of greater than 8 h resulting in a cumulative dose of >4 g day-1." Wolf 2012, Abstract: "23.8 % of participants demonstrated they would overdose on a single over-the-counter acetaminophen product by exceeding a dose of four grams in a 24-hour period".
claims.location: Reid: Introduction. Craig: Methods. Wolf: Abstract.
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults / standard therapeutic paracetamol dosing / 24 hours
claims.safe_wording: For most adults the usual maximum is 4 g of paracetamol in 24 hours. With 500 mg tablets, that is 8 tablets a day, counting every product that contains paracetamol.
claims.qualifications: The BNF and product labels were not opened; the 4 g standard is taken from published papers. '8 tablets' is derived arithmetic (4 g divided by 500 mg). Lower maximums may apply to some people (see C10-09-f).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: See C10-09-f on low body weight and frailty.

numbers.meaning: standard adult maximum daily paracetamol dose

claims.claim: Taking two paracetamol-containing products at once is a recognised route to accidental excess: in a US study nearly half of adults said they would take two such products together, and about 1 in 5 accidental paracetamol overdose calls to an Australian poisons centre involved more than one product.
claims.supporting_passage: Wolf 2012, Abstract: "In addition, 45.6 % of adults demonstrated they would overdose by 'double-dipping' with two acetaminophen-containing products." Table 4, Double-dipping with 2 products by age: "18-30 37.1; 31-45 44.1; 46-60 52.8; 61-80 40.0" (P = 0.05). Discussion: "Clearly, our study is limited by the fact that the assessments of individuals' misunderstanding and misuse of OTC acetaminophen products reflects hypothetical and not actual health behaviors." Chidiac 2024, Results 3.1: "Multiple paracetamol-containing products (which may include more than one brand of the same category) were taken in 2816 (19.6%) exposures"; Abstract: "The in-depth analysis of exposures recorded during 2021 revealed 1899 exposures (median age 46 years, 63.4% female) with 26.8% requiring hospitalisation." ... "6% of exposures developed hepatotoxicity." Table 1: "Elderly >=75 years: Entire cohort: 1733 (12.1%)".
claims.location: Wolf: Abstract, Table 4, Discussion. Chidiac: Abstract, Results 3.1, Table 1.
claims.pico_timeframe: Wolf: 500 US primary care adults aged 18 to 80 / simulated choice to take two acetaminophen products together / single interview. Chidiac: 14,380 unintentional paracetamol dosing-error calls, people aged 12 and over, New South Wales, 2017 to 2023.
claims.safe_wording: Doubling up is easy to do. In a US study, nearly half of 500 adults, shown real shop products, said it would be safe to take two paracetamol-containing products together; among those aged 61 to 80 it was 4 in 10. At an Australian poisons centre, about 1 in 5 calls about accidentally taking too much paracetamol involved more than one paracetamol product.
claims.qualifications: Wolf measured what people said they would do, not what they did, and used US products. Chidiac counts calls, not confirmed harm; hospitalisation and liver-injury figures apply to all ages in 2021, not older people specifically. Neither study is UK-based. Do not say accidental excess 'in older people is often' a counting problem: no source gives that proportion for older people.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No UK or older-people-specific data on how often double-dosing happens were found.

numbers.meaning: of 500 US adults aged 18 to 80, demonstrated they would exceed the maximum by taking two acetaminophen products (simulated task)
same outcome among participants aged 61 to 80 (Wolf Table 4; group size not reported)
Australian poisons centre dosing-error calls involving more than one paracetamol product, 2017 to 2023
of those calls concerned people aged 75 or over
2021 calls (all ages, n = 1899) needing hospital care; exposures developing liver injury

claims.claim: In a Scottish liver unit series of adults with severe paracetamol liver injury, about 1 in 4 had taken too much over several doses rather than at once, and pain relief was the commonest reason among them.
claims.supporting_passage: Abstract: "Between 1992 and 2008, 663 patients were admitted with paracetamol-induced severe liver injury, of whom 161 (24.3%) had taken a staggered overdose. Staggered overdose patients were significantly older and more likely to abuse alcohol than single time point overdose patients. Relief of pain (58.2%) was the commonest rationale for repeated supratherapeutic ingestion." ... "had higher mortality rates compared with single time point overdoses (37.3% vs. 27.8%, P= 0.025), although this overdose pattern did not independently predict death." Results: "Staggered overdose subjects were significantly older (median 39 (29-46) years) compared with single overdose patients (32 (24-43) years, P < 0.001)" ... "Information regarding the reasons for overdose was available for 134/161 (83.2%) of staggered overdoses. The most common (58.2%) rationale for overdose was for relief of pain" ... "A total of 46/134 (34.3%) of staggered overdoses were taken deliberately as a suicide attempt." Table 1: "Age (years): 34 (26-44)".
claims.location: Abstract; Results (Single time point vs staggered overdoses; Repeated supratherapeutic overdoses and pain); Tables 1 and 2
claims.pico_timeframe: 663 adults (median age 34) with severe paracetamol liver injury, Scottish Liver Transplantation Unit / staggered vs single time point overdose / reasons, outcomes / 1992 to 2008
claims.safe_wording: In a Scottish liver unit, 663 adults were admitted with severe liver damage from paracetamol between 1992 and 2008. About 1 in 4 had taken too much over several doses rather than all at once. Where the reason was known, the most common was trying to relieve pain (78 of 134). Most people in this series were young or middle-aged adults.
claims.qualifications: State that this was a series of adults of all ages (median 34; staggered group median 39), not older people; do not use 'older' from the abstract. A third of the staggered group were suicide attempts and many misused alcohol. Do not imply that doubling up commonly causes liver failure in older people. Mortality difference was not independent of other factors; do not present it as caused by the staggered pattern.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Single specialist unit, referral bias toward the most severe cases; data from 1992 to 2008.

numbers.meaning: adults admitted with severe paracetamol liver injury, 1992 to 2008
staggered overdoses among 663
pain relief as the reason, among staggered overdoses with a recorded reason
staggered overdoses that were suicide attempts
age of staggered vs single overdose patients
mortality, staggered vs single overdose (not independently predictive)

claims.claim: For people who are frail or weigh under 50 kg, a lower daily paracetamol maximum is often advised, though the safest dose has not been established; full adult doses are common in this group.
claims.supporting_passage: Reid 2022, Abstract: "Paracetamol doses administered in hospital, and doses prescribed on discharge, were compared against consensus guidelines that recommended <=60 mg/kg/d for older people weighing <50 kg, and <=3000 mg/d for frail older people." ... "In total, 240 admissions (n = 229 patients, mean age 84.7 years) were analysed. During 150 (62.5%) admissions, higher than recommended paracetamol doses were prescribed. On 138 (57.5%) occasions, patients were prescribed paracetamol on discharge, and 112/138 (81.2%) doses were higher than recommended." Introduction: "For example, England's Healthcare Safety Investigation Branch, an organisation responsible for the investigating patient safety concerns, is conducting an investigation titled Unintentional overdose of paracetamol in adults with low body weight. This was prompted by reports of paracetamol overdose in patients with low body weight at therapeutic doses." Discussion: "Although there is limited evidence that the standard maximum therapeutic dose (4 g/d) leads to significant rates of liver injury in frail and low-weight older people, we believe that reduced doses should be considered for 3 reasons." Caparrotta 2018, Abstract: "The safe (and still effective) oral dose of paracetamol in patients weighing less than 50 kg has not been established." ... "There is no patient group that is unequivocally at elevated risk of paracetamol-induced liver toxicity."
claims.location: Reid: Abstract, Introduction, Discussion. Caparrotta: Abstract.
claims.pico_timeframe: Reid: 229 inpatients aged 70 or over (mean 84.7) who were frail or under 50 kg, Melbourne, 2018 / paracetamol dose vs consensus guideline / hospital stay and discharge. Caparrotta: literature on risk factors for paracetamol liver injury.
claims.safe_wording: If you weigh under 50 kg (about 7 stone 12 lb) or are frail, ask a pharmacist or doctor whether a lower daily maximum is right for you. Some guidelines advise a lower dose for people in this group, although research has not established the safest dose. In one Australian study of frail or low-weight hospital patients aged 70 and over, about 8 in 10 discharge prescriptions were above those guideline doses.
claims.qualifications: Do not quote or cite the BNF: its exact wording for adults under 50 kg was not opened. The consensus guidelines in Reid are Australian. England's HSIB investigation is reported via Reid, not opened. Evidence that 4 g a day harms low-weight older people is limited (Reid; Caparrotta), so frame lower doses as a precaution, not as proven necessary. '7 stone 12 lb' is a unit conversion of 50 kg.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Caparrotta 2018: no group is unequivocally at higher risk; safe dose under 50 kg not established.

claims.claim: Paracetamol packs advise against taking other paracetamol-containing products at the same time.
claims.supporting_passage: No passage opened. UK pack labelling, the BNF and MHRA pages could not be opened from this environment.
claims.safe_wording: Do not state what pack labels say. Advise readers to check the ingredients of every product and ask a pharmacist.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Chidiac 2024 notes that labelling changes in Canada did not reduce hospital admissions for accidental overdose.

candidates.reason: All essential claims can be supported, but three parts of the draft need to change. (1) The draft opening line says quinine 'is no longer a routine prescription in the UK', but Acheampong 2013 found prescribing in England 'remains common' after the 2010 advice. (2) The stretching claim rests on one positive trial; the 2021 Cochrane review and a UK trial found mixed or no benefit. (3) The MHRA 2010 wording could only be found in a search extract, so the restriction must be attributed to opened sources: the Age and Ageing review, UK prescribing advice as reported by Cochrane, and Man-Son-Hing. The quinine effect is now available as absolute numbers: about 9 cramps per fortnight on placebo, 2 to 3 fewer on quinine.
candidates.revised_angle: If quinine is on your repeat list for night cramps, ask when it was last reviewed. In trials, quinine cut cramps from about 9 to about 6 or 7 a fortnight (low-quality evidence). Minor side effects were more common on quinine, and rare serious harms include a fall in platelets, heart rhythm problems and death in overdose. Specialist advice is to keep quinine for severe cramps, allow up to 4 weeks to see an effect, and pause it every few months to check it still helps. In an English GP trial, advice to try stopping quinine led about 1 in 4 more people to stop, and the trial did not show a clear rise in cramps. Also ask whether another medicine could be contributing: some water tablets and long-acting inhalers are linked with cramps. Calf and hamstring stretching is harmless in trials and reasonable to try, but its benefit is uncertain.

candidates.reason: The core check (add up paracetamol across every product) is supported, but the evidence base and wording need to change. Craig 2012 was a series of adults of all ages: median age 34, and 39 in the staggered group, which the abstract calls 'older'. It cannot support a point about older people and may only be used as an all-ages example. No source shows that accidental excess 'in older people is often' a counting problem. The BNF advice for people under 50 kg and UK pack-label wording could not be opened. Doubling-up is better supported by Wolf 2012 (simulated, US; 40% of people aged 61 to 80) and Chidiac 2024 (about 1 in 5 accidental-excess calls involved more than one product). The low-weight caution is supported by Reid 2022, with the uncertainty noted by Caparrotta 2018.
candidates.revised_angle: Paracetamol is in more packets than the ones labelled paracetamol: co-codamol, co-dydramol and some cold and flu remedies all contain it. Taking two of these together, each as directed, can take the total over the usual 4 g daily maximum. In a US study nearly half of adults, and 4 in 10 of those aged 61 to 80, said they would do this when shown real products. About 1 in 5 accidental-excess calls to an Australian poisons centre involved more than one paracetamol product. People who are frail or weigh under 50 kg may be advised a lower maximum, though the safest dose is not established. Actions: add up paracetamol across every product, including those bought from shops, and ask a pharmacist. Clinicians reviewing pain relief should ask about bought medicines. If the Scottish liver unit series is used, say it was of adults of all ages.
